'''''Vachellia farnesiana''''', also known as '''''Acacia farnesiana''''', and previously '''''Mimosa farnesiana''''', commonly known as '''sweet acacia''',<ref name=VAFA>{{PLANTS|id=VAFA|taxon=Vachellia farnesiana|access-date=25 March 2016}}</ref> '''huisache''',<ref name=LadyBird>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=ACFA|title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin|website=www.wildflower.org|access-date=2016-06-28}}</ref> '''casha tree''', or '''needle bush''', is a species of shrub or small tree in the [[legume]] family, [[Fabaceae]]. Its flowers are used in the perfume industry.

== Description ==
The plant is [[deciduous]] over part of its range,<ref>[http://cals.arizona.edu/pubs/crops/az1359/az13592b.pdf PDF] Ursula K. Schuch and Margaret Norem, Growth of Legume Tree Species Growing in the Southwestern United States, University of Arizona.</ref> but [[evergreen]] in most locales.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://pick5.pick.uga.edu/mp/20q?search=Acacia+farnesiana&guide=North_American_Invasives |title=Discover Life - Fabaceae: Acacia farnesiana (L. ) Willd. - Cassie Flower, Vachellia farnesiana, Poponax farnesiana, Mimosa farnesiana, Ellington Curse, Klu, Sweet Acacia, Mimosa Bush, Huisache |publisher=Pick5.pick.uga.edu |access-date=2012-04-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224075703/http://pick5.pick.uga.edu/mp/20q?search=Acacia+farnesiana&guide=North_American_Invasives |archive-date=2012-02-24 }}</ref> Growing from multiple trunks, it reaches a height of {{Convert|15|-|30|ft|m|abbr=off|order=flip}}.<ref name="LadyBird" /> The bark is whitish gray.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=U.S. Department of the Army |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T2p7DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA8 |title=The Official U.S. Army Illustrated Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Lyons Press]] |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-4930-4039-1 |location=Guilford, CT |page=8 |oclc=1043567121}}</ref> The base of each [[leaf]] is accompanied by a pair of thorns on the branch.<ref name="Uvalde">{{Cite web |url=http://agrilife.org/herbarium/trees-shrubs-and-vines/trees-shrubs-common-name-index/huisache/ |title=Sweet Acacia (''Acacia farnesiana'') |work=Native Plants of South Texas |publisher=Texas AgriLife Research and Extension |access-date=2009-06-30 |archive-date=2014-01-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140114031500/http://agrilife.org/herbarium/trees-shrubs-and-vines/trees-shrubs-common-name-index/huisache/ }}</ref> The dark brown fruit is a [[seed pod]].<ref name=":0" />

== Taxonomy ==
=== Taxonomic history ===
It was first described by Europeans under the name ''Acacia Indica Farnesiana'' in 1625 by Tobias Aldini from plants grown in [[Rome]] in the [[Farnese Gardens]] from seed collected in [[Santo Domingo]], in what is now the [[Dominican Republic]], which germinated in 1611. Aldini included an illustration of the plant, which he contrasted with an illustration of the first known ''Acacia''; ''Acacia nilotica''. This first (European) illustration of the plant was later designated as the (lecto-)type.<ref name="Bell">{{cite journal |last1=Bell |first1=Karen L. |last2=Rangan |first2=Haripriya |last3=Fernandes |first3=Manuel M. |last4=Kull |first4=Christian A. |last5=Murphy |first5=Daniel J. |date=12 April 2017 |title=Chance long-distance or human-mediated dispersal? How Acacia s.l. farnesiana attained its pan-tropical distribution |journal=Royal Society Open Science |volume=4 |issue=4 |article-number=170105 |bibcode=2017RSOS....470105B |doi=10.1098/rsos.170105  |doi-access=free|pmc=5414274 |pmid=28484637}}</ref><ref name="Árboles">{{cite book |last1=Little |first1=Elbert Luther |last2=Wadsworth |first2=Frank H. |last3=Marrero |first3=José |date=1977 |title=Árboles comunes de Puerto Rico y las Islas Vírgenes |url=http://edicionesdigitales.info/biblioteca/arbolesprvi1esp.pdf |pages=145–147 |language=es |location=San Juan |publisher=La Editorial de la Universidad de Puerto Rico |isbn=978-0-8477-0383-8}}</ref> In 1753, [[Carl Linnaeus]] used Aldini's work as basis for his [[taxon]] ''Mimosa farnesiana''. In 1806 [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow]] moved this taxon to the genus ''Acacia''.<ref name="IPNI1">{{Cite book |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=470307-1&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3Dacacia%2Bfarnesiana%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |volume=4 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=13 July 2018}}</ref>

Partly due to its wide distributional range, the taxon has attracted many synonyms. Especially in the [[United States]], the taxonomy has been confused.

In 1809, Willdenow described ''Acacia acicularis'' from [[Central America]] collected and named during Humboldt and Bonpland's scientific expedition to the [[Americas]].<ref name="IPNI2">{{Cite book |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=469632-1&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DAcacia%2Bacicularis%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=13 July 2018}}</ref> ''Acacia ferox'' was described in 1843 in Belgium from collections in [[Mexico]].<ref name="IPNI3">{{Cite book |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=470316-1&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DAcacia%2Bferox%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=13 July 2018}}</ref> ''Acacia lenticellata'' was described in 1859 for the plants found growing throughout [[Australia]].<ref name="IPNI4">{{cite web |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=69646-3&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DAcacia%2Blenticellata%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=14 July 2018}}</ref>

In the ''Prodromus Florae Peninsulae Indiae Orientalis'' of 1834, Wight & Arnott, attempted to split the burgeoning genus ''Acacia'' by moving a number of the ''Acacia'' species growing in [[India]] to the new genus ''Vachellia''.

This was not widely followed, nonetheless in 1933, Small verified Alexander's name ''Vachellia densiflora'' for plants growing in [[Louisiana]], and awarded ''V. peninsularis'' and ''V. insularis'' to different populations of the plants growing in [[Florida]].<ref name="PlantList1" />

In 1936, Cory moved ''Vachellia densiflora'' to ''Acacia densiflora'', but as this name had already been used for another taxon, and was therefore invalidated ''sensu'' Cory, in 1969, this taxon was renamed ''A. smallii'' by Isely. In 1948, F. J. Herm. synonymised ''Vachellia peninsularis'' and ''V. insularis'' under ''Acacia pinetorum''.<ref name="PlantList1" /><ref name="VAFA" />

In 1933, M. E. Jones named plants he collected in Mexico ''Pithecellobium minutum''. This taxon was moved to ''Acacia minuta'' by R.'' ''Mitchel Beauchamp in 1980. Beauchamp also subsumed ''A. smallii'' under ''A. minuta'' subsp. ''densiflora'', although this was not widely followed.

''Acacia smallii'' was used in the U.S. for the 'native' ''A. farnesiana'' growing in the drylands west of Louisiana, but at the same time, the taxon ''A. farnesiana'' was recognised in the U.S. for purportedly imported non-native plants originally cultivated in the Southeastern U.S. as ornamentals and later thought naturalised there. Additionally, in Florida, ''A. pinetorum'' was recognised as a rare endemic native.<ref name="VAFA" />

A paper in 1989 by H. D. Clarke, D. S. Seigler and J. E. Ebinger finally cleared up some of this confusion, synonymising ''Acacia smallii'' and a number of other taxa under the nominate form of ''A. farnesiana'', under which they also included all of the plants growing outside of the Americas. In the same paper, they recognised ''A. farnesiana'' var. ''guanacastensis'' from herbarium collections made by D. H. Janzen in 1976 in Guanacaste, [[Costa Rica]].<ref name="Clarke">Clarke, H.D., Seigler, D.S., Ebinger, J.E. 1989; 'Acacia farnesiana (Fabaceae: Mimosoideae) and Related Species from Mexico, the Southwestern U.S., and the Caribbean' Systematic Botany 14 549-564</ref><ref name="IPNI5">{{Cite book |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=271485-2&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DVachellia%2Bguanacastensis%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |volume=14 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=14 July 2018}}</ref> This taxon was later elevated to species status as ''A. guanacastensis'' by the same three in 2000<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=1087113-2&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DVachellia%2Bguanacastensis%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |volume=25 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=14 July 2018}}</ref> and later moved to ''Vachellia guanacastensis'' by Seigler and Ebinger in 2006.<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/simplePlantNameSearch.do?find_wholeName=Vachellia+guanacastensis&output_format=normal&query_type=by_query&back_page=query_ipni.html |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |volume=87 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=14 July 2018}}</ref>

''Acacia pinetorum'' was subsumed under ''A. farnesiana'' as ''A. farnesiana'' subsp. ''pinetorum'' in 2002 by Clarke, Seigler and Ebinger (rendering the nominate form ''A. farnesiana'' subsp. ''farnesiana'').<ref name="IPNI6">{{Cite book |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=20005572-1&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditSimplePlantNameSearch.do%3Ffind_wholeName%3DAcacia%2Bpinetorum%26output_format%3Dnormal |title=IPNI Plant Name Details |volume=47 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=23 April 2015 |publisher=The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) |access-date=14 July 2018 |quote=note the Plant List & Tropicos database citation records incomplete authorship}}</ref> Seigler and Ebinger later reclassified this as ''Vachellia farnesiana'' var. ''pinetorum'' in 2005.<ref name="PlantList1" />

=== Infraspecific diversity ===
''Acacia farnesiana'' var. ''guanacastensis'' is primarily distinguished by larger leaflets. It remains controversial; most taxonomic authorities in Mexico and Central America recognise this taxon as a full species under either ''A. guanacastensis'' or ''Vachellia guanacastensis'', the ''Árboles nativos e introduciados de El Salvador'' of 2009 subsumed it under ''Acacia farnesiana''. It is recognised as present in Costa Rica, El Salvador, [[Guatemala]], [[Nicaragua]], and the southern [[Gulf of Mexico|Gulf]] and southwestern regions of Mexico by the ''Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families'' (2018), but whether the taxon as recognised by the different authorities replaces ''Acacia farnesiana'' in Central America (but not the [[Caribbean]] or [[South America]]) or exists [[Sympatry|sympatrically]] remains unclear. This has implications for the classification of the extra-American distribution of ''A. farnesiana'' as the populations growing in Australia and the [[Philippines]] have recently (2017) been shown to derive from ancient Central American origins.

''Acacia pinetorum'', the pineland acacia or pineland wattle,<ref name="VAFA" /> is also disputed. The International Legume Database and Information Service continues to recognise ''A. pinetorum'',<ref name="PlantList1" /> while the [[U.S. Department of Agriculture]] recognises ''V. farnesiana'' var. ''pinetorum''.<ref name="VAFA" />

In France, two old cultivars have been developed for the perfume industry. These were also recognised as varieties at one time.

=== Etymology ===
The [[species|specific]] name ''farnesiana'' honors [[Odoardo Farnese (cardinal)|Odoardo Farnese]] (1573–1626) of the notable Italian [[House of Farnese|Farnese]] family, which after 1550, under the patronage of Cardinal [[Alessandro Farnese (cardinal)|Alessandro Farnese]], maintained some of the first private European botanical gardens in Rome, the [[Farnese Gardens]], in the 16th and 17th centuries.

This acacia was first described from these gardens, imported to Italy from Santo Domingo, in what is now the Dominican Republic.<ref>{{cite web |title=Etymology of farnesol, accessed August 27, 2009 |url=http://dictionary.reference.com/browse/farnesol |access-date=2012-04-19 |publisher=Dictionary.reference.com}}</ref><ref name="swsbm.com">{{cite journal |last=Fluckiger |first=F. A. |date=March 1885 |title=The Essential Oil Industry in Grasse |url=http://www.swsbm.com/AJP/AJP_1885_No_3.pdf |volume=57 |issue=3 |access-date=2012-04-19 |journal=American Journal of Pharmacy}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Location of the Farnese family gardens, now known only as a remnant |url=http://www.gardenvisit.com/garden/farnese_gardens |access-date=2012-04-19 |publisher=Gardenvisit.com}}</ref><ref name="Bell" />

Analysis of essences of the floral extract from this plant, long used in perfumery, resulted in the name for the [[sesquiterpene]] biosynthetic chemical [[farnesol]], found as a basic sterol precursor in plants, and cholesterol precursor in animals.<ref name="swsbm.com" />{{Failed verification|date=June 2021}}

The name '''huisache''' of Mexico and [[Texas]] is derived from [[Nahuatl]] and means "many thorns".<ref name="LadyBird" />
The Australian name '''needle bush''' came about because of the numerous thorns distributed along its branches.

== Distribution and habitat ==
Of all ''Acacia'' species, this plant has the greatest distribution. It was first described by Europeans in 1625 by Tobias Aldini from plants grown from seed collected in Santo Domingo, in what is now the Dominican Republic. The native range of ''V. farnesiana'' has been or is sometimes disputed. While the point of origin is thought to be the Caribbean, the [[Guianas]], Mexico, and/or [[Central America]], the species has a pantropical distribution incorporating most of the Americas (from the Southern U.S. to Chile, excluding the [[Amazon River|Amazon]]), most of Australia, much of [[Africa]], southern Europe, and southern [[Asia]]. In the Caribbean, it is present from the [[Bahamas]] and [[Cuba]] south to [[Trinidad]], [[Curaçao]], and [[Aruba]], where in it is believed to be native to [[Hispaniola]] and certainly Cuba, but possibly native or naturalised elsewhere. In the U.S., it is thought to be native to southern Texas, southern [[New Mexico]], southern [[Arizona]], and southern California, but perhaps naturalized in southern Louisiana, coastal [[Mississippi]], coastal [[Alabama]], coastal [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], and southern Florida. Whether the extra-American distribution is natural (the seed pods have probably floated across the Pacific) or anthropogenic remains disputed. It was introduced to Europe, the [[Middle East]], India, Africa, and recently [[Gran Canaria]] and [[Hawaii]]. It has long been thought to be native to the Philippines and Australia, having spread there by natural means, because plants were collected there before colonisation in 1788, it was distributed throughout the country, indigenous knowledge on the plant is extensive, and 2017 [[DNA]] investigations show this as most likely. In Australia, however, the government now considers it as non-native or even [[Invasive species in Australia|invasive]].<ref name="VAFA" /><ref name="Bell" /><ref name="Árboles" /><ref name="Clarke" /><ref name="purdue">{{cite web|url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/duke_energy/Acacia_farnesiana.html |title=Purdue University |publisher=Hort.purdue.edu |date=1997-12-16 |access-date=2012-04-19}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=20739&PTRefFk=8500000 |title=The Euro+Med PlantBase Project |access-date=7 July 2018}}</ref><ref name="keyserver">{{cite web |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/vachellia_farnesiana.htm |title=Vachellia farnesiana |access-date=7 July 2018}}</ref>

The plant prefers full sunlight in a [[tropical climate]].<ref name=":0" />

== Ecology ==
[[Deer]] and [[Peccary|peccaries]] eat its fruit, various [[bird]]s use the plant for nesting and cover, and insects eat the [[nectar]] from its flowers. If disturbed, it readily resprouts.<ref name="Uvalde"/>  It thrives in dry, [[Soil salinity|saline]], or sodic soils.

It is considered a serious pest plant in parts of Australia, as it interferes with cattle-ranching operations. It readily spreads in commercial grazing pastures, especially along creeks, which might affect ease of transport for farmers, complicates muster, and can damage farm machinery. The seeds are dispersed by cattle after they eat the nutritious pods, and growth is promoted by overgrazing. Numerous herbicides are used to control it on ranches; chemical control is the only way to kill it.<ref name=keyserver/><ref>{{cite web
 |url          = http://www.northwestweeds.nsw.gov.au/mimosa_bush.htm

 |publisher    = Northwestweeds.nsw.gov.au

 |archive-date = 2008-01-28
 }}</ref><ref name=weeds>{{cite web |url=http://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/219 |title=Mimosa bush (Vachellia farnesiana) - NSW WeedWise |access-date=7 July 2018 |archive-date=30 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230430013923/https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/219 }}</ref><ref name=Hawaii>{{cite web |url=http://www.botany.hawaii.edu/faculty/cw_smith/aca_far.htm |title=Acacia farnesiana - Alien Plants of Hawaii, UH Botany |access-date=7 July 2018}}</ref> The plant has been spread to many new locations as a result of human activity, and it is considered a serious [[weed]] in [[Fiji]], where locals call it Ellington's curse.

== Uses ==
=== Perfume ===
The flowers are processed through [[distillation]] to produce a [[perfume]] called cassie, which has been described as "delicious".<ref name=Sturt>{{cite book|title=Sturtevant's notes on edible plants|date=1919|page=19|url=https://archive.org/details/sturtevantsnotes00sturuoft|publisher=Albany : J.B. Lyon|isbn=978-0-486-20459-8 }}</ref><ref name=WildflowersIsrael>{{cite web |url=http://www.wildflowers.co.il/english/plant.asp?ID=1459 |title=Sweet Acacia, Needle bush Medicinal, introduce, allergenic |last=Eshel |first=Amram |website=Wildflowers of Israel |publisher=israelbiz- בניית אתרים |access-date=11 July 2018 |archive-date=11 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180711193207/http://www.wildflowers.co.il/english/plant.asp?ID=1459 }}</ref> It is widely used in the perfume industry in [[Europe]]. Flowers of the plant provide the perfume essence from which the biologically important [[sesquiterpenoid]] [[farnesol]] is named.<ref name=WildflowersIsrael/>

Scented [[ointment]]s from cassie are made in India.<ref name=WildflowersIsrael/>

=== Gum ===
It exudes a [[natural gum|gum]], which is sometimes collected.<ref name=Sturt/>

=== Tanning Leather ===
{{See also|Catechu}}
The bark is used for its [[tannin]] content.<ref name="purdue" /><ref name="WildflowersIsrael" /> The concentration of tannin in the seed pods is about 23%.<ref name="WildflowersIsrael" /> Highly tannic barks are common in general to acacias.  Extracts of many are used in medicine for this reason.

=== Food ===
The plant's young leaves, flowers, and seed pods are edible raw or cooked.<ref name=":0" />

=== Fodder and forage ===
The foliage is a significant source of [[Fodder|forage]] in much of its range, with a [[protein]] content around 18%.<ref name=WildflowersIsrael/>
The tree makes good forage for bees.<ref name=WildflowersIsrael/>
The seed pods are readily eaten by livestock.<ref>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=514}}</ref>

=== Ornamental ===
This [[drought-tolerant]] species is often used in [[xeriscaping]] in Texas.<ref name="Uvalde"/>

=== Dyes and inks ===
A black pigment is extracted from the bark and fruit.<ref name=WildflowersIsrael/>

=== Traditional medicine ===
In [[Brazil]], some people use the seeds of ''V. farnesiana'' to kill [[rabies|rabid]] [[dog]]s.<ref name="purdue"/> ''V. farnesiana'' has been used in [[Colombia]] to treat [[malaria]], and in one ''[[in vitro]]'' study, an [[ethanol]] extract from the leaves showed some activity against the malarial [[pathogen]] ''[[Plasmodium falciparum]]'' with an IC<sub>50</sub> value of 1 to 2 [[microgram]]/[[millilitre]] (as did almost everything tested), though it showed no activity in [[animal model]]s or a [[ferriprotoporphyrin]] biomineralization inhibition test.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Garavito | first1 = G. | last2 = Rincón | first2 = J. | last3 = Arteaga | first3 = L. | last4 = Hata | first4 = Y. | last5 = Bourdy | first5 = G. | last6 = Gimenez | first6 = A. | last7 = Pinzón | first7 = R. | last8 = Deharo | first8 = E. | doi=10.1016/j.jep.2006.03.033 |title=Antimalarial activity of some Colombian medicinal plants |journal = Journal of Ethnopharmacology | volume = 107 | issue = 3 | pages = 460–462 | year = 2006 | pmid =  16713157}}</ref> In the Philippines the leaves are traditionally rubbed on the skin to treat skin diseases in livestock.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stuartxchange.org/HerbsAnimalsSkin.html |title=Philippine Herbs Used in Small Animal Practice |last=Santiago-Flores |first=M. Leila |publisher=Stuartxchange.org |access-date=2012-04-19}}</ref> In [[Malaysia]], an infusion of the plant's flowers and leaves is mixed with turmeric for [[post-partum]] treatment.<ref name=Samy>{{ cite book | first1=Joseph | last1=Samy | first2=Sugumaran | last2=Manickam | year=2005 | title=Herbs of Malaysia | publisher=Times Editions | page=29 | isbn=978-983-3001-79-8 }}</ref>
